query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single heat‐treatment step that triggers controlled, in‐situ precipitation of a ductile, coherent secondary phase within the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 matrix will greatly improve its mechanical integrity (i.e. crack resistance and compressive strength) without substantially reducing its field‐driven caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a large caloric response but poor mechanical integrity (i.e. tendency to crack).
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored heat-treatment protocol (controlled annealing below the primary phase melting point) to induce the in-situ formation of a finely dispersed, ductile secondary phase.
generation.conditions: Under applied magnetic or pressure fields and over the relevant temperature range of the caloric transition, with loading regimes similar to those used in prior mechanical tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanometer- to sub-micron-scale, coherent secondary phase precipitates (e.g., Mn-rich or similar ductile intermetallic phases) distributed along grain boundaries and within grain interiors.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as crack arrestors and bridge microcracks to enhance toughness and compressive strength while their coherent nature minimizes any disturbance to the magnetic/magneto-structural transition responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy’s compressive strength is expected to increase (e.g., on the order of a 25-50% improvement relative to the unmodified state) while the magnitude of the caloric response remains within ±10% of its original value.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits high caloric response but poor mechanical integrity with crack formation under load.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when the heat-treatment conditions (temperature and time) are carefully controlled to promote uniform, coherent precipitation without forming deleterious secondary phases, and within the operational range of applied magnetic/pressure fields and temperatures where the original caloric transition occurs.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum volume fraction, size, and distribution of the precipitates required to balance mechanical reinforcement with minimal interference in the caloric behavior are not precisely known; further optimization may be needed to fully validate the intervention.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one set serves as the control and the other undergoes the designed heat-treatment treatment to induce in-situ precipitation. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM/SEM for precipitate identification), measure compressive strength (under standardized mechanical tests) and quantify the caloric response (under applied field and/or pressure) across the temperature range of interest.
measurements: Caloric effect magnitude (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change) under applied magnetic/pressure fields
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (≥25%) in compressive strength compared to controls, OR if the caloric response is reduced by more than 10% relative to the unmodified alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Rare-Earth-Zirconate Porous High-Entropy Ceramics with Unique Pore Structures for Thermal Insulating Applications

Abstract: Porous high-entropy ceramics are a new alternative material for thermal insulation. Their better stability and low thermal conductivity are due to lattice distortion and unique pore structures. In this work, rare-earth-zirconate ((La0.25Eu0.25Gd0.25Yb0.25)2(Zr0.75Ce0.25)2O7) porous high-entropy ceramics were fabricated by a tert-butyl alcohol (TBA)-based gel-casting method. The regulation of pore structures was realized through changing different initial solid loadings. The XRD, HRTEM, and SAED results showed that the porous high-entropy ceramics had a single fluorite phase without impurity phases, exhibiting high porosity (67.1–81.5%), relatively high compressive strength (1.02–6.45 MPa) and low thermal conductivity (0.0642–0.1213 W/(m·K)) at room temperature. Porous high-entropy ceramics with 81.5% porosity demonstrated excellent thermal properties, showing a thermal conductivity of 0.0642 W/(m·K) at room temperature and 0.1467 W/(m·K) at 1200 °C.
